subsection: 10. Case study: the Montgomery bus boycott, 1956

notes.b: Montgomery, Alabama, enforced racial segregation on its buses by city ordinance, and black passengers, who made up most of the riders, were required to give up their seats to white passengers.
points: Montgomery's city buses reserved the front rows for white passengers, and the driver could move the dividing line backwards to make more room for white riders, forcing black passengers to stand.
Black riders made up the large majority of bus passengers in Montgomery, so the segregation rules affected most of the city's working population.

Earlier protests had failed to change the rules: in March 1955 Claudette Colvin, a fifteen-year-old schoolgirl, was arrested for refusing to give up her seat, and local black leaders decided not to make her case a test case.
The Montgomery Improvement Association had been planning a challenge to the bus system before Parks' arrest, and the local NAACP and women's groups had been discussing a boycott.

notes.h: The arrest of Rosa Parks and the boycott begins
notes.b: The arrest of Rosa Parks on 1 December 1955 became the spark for a boycott that lasted over a year.
points: Rosa Parks, a seamstress and the secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP, was arrested on 1 December 1955 after refusing to give up her seat to a white passenger.
E. D. Nixon, president of the Montgomery NAACP, bailed Parks out of jail, and he and others arranged for her case to be challenged in court.
The Women's Political Council, led by Jo Ann Robinson, distributed leaflets on the night of 1 December calling for a one-day boycott of the buses on Monday, 5 December 1955.
The boycott was a success on its first day, and a mass meeting at the Holt Street Baptist Church that evening voted to continue the boycott until demands were met.

The demands were modest: courteous treatment, seating on a first-come, first-served basis with black passengers filling seats from the back, and the hiring of black drivers on routes serving black areas.

notes.h: Organising the boycott: the Montgomery Improvement Association
notes.b: The Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA) co-ordinated the boycott, and its car pool and church networks kept the city's black population off the buses.
points: The MIA was formed on 5 December 1955, and the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr., a young pastor of the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, was elected its president.
King's speeches at mass meetings combined a demand for justice with a commitment to non-violence, and they helped to hold together a movement of ministers, domestic workers and students.
A system of car pools, run by volunteers and taxi drivers charging a reduced fare, took black passengers to work and school, and churches and businesses provided additional transport.
Black walkers were common in Montgomery during the boycott, and the sight of thousands of people walking long distances to work became a symbol of the movement's determination.

notes.h: White resistance and the legal challenge
notes.b: Montgomery's white authorities responded with arrests, violence and legal action, but the boycott's legal challenge eventually reached the Supreme Court.
points: King was arrested in February 1956 for organising the boycott, under a state law banning boycotts, and his arrest attracted national press coverage.
On 30 January 1956 a bomb was thrown at King's house during the boycott, and a crowd gathered outside, but King appealed for calm.

The city authorities and the White Citizens' Council pressed for the car pool system to be banned, and a state court injunction in early 1956 ordered the car pools to stop operating in their existing form.
Four black women, including Claudette Colvin and Aurelia Browder, filed a case in February 1956 challenging the constitutionality of Alabama's bus segregation laws in Browder v Gayle.
A federal district court ruled the bus segregation laws unconstitutional in June 1956, and the state appealed to the Supreme Court, which affirmed the ruling on 13 November 1956.
The formal order from the Supreme Court reached Montgomery in December 1956, and the boycott was called off on 20 December 1956 after 381 days.

notes.b: The boycott ended bus segregation in Montgomery, but its wider effects depended on how far the movement could extend its success.
points: Montgomery's buses were desegregated on 21 December 1956, and black and white passengers rode together for the first time under the city's new rules.
The boycott was the first large-scale test of non-violent protest against segregation, and its success drew national and international attention to the movement.
In January 1957 the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC) was formed by King and other ministers to co-ordinate church-based protest across the South.
Segregation remained in schools, housing and most public places in Montgomery, so the victory was limited to one aspect of public life.

notes.h: Significance: King, non-violence and the movement
notes.b: Historians see the Montgomery bus boycott as the starting point of the mass civil rights movement, and it made King its most prominent leader.
points: Non-violence was adopted as the movement's principle, and King drew on the teachings of Gandhi and the Christian tradition of love and forgiveness.
The boycott showed that black communities could organise economic pressure on segregation, a method that was later used in other cities.
The role of women, including Rosa Parks, Jo Ann Robinson and the Women's Political Council, was crucial, though men were more often given public recognition.
The boycott led to the founding of the SCLC and to King's rise as the national leader of the civil rights movement.

notes.h: Violence and the wider Alabama response, 1956
notes.b: The boycott provoked a campaign of intimidation across Alabama, and it showed how far white authorities would go to protect segregation.
points: The home of Robert Graetz, a white minister who supported the boycott, was bombed in January 1956, and the bombing was one of several attacks on the movement's supporters.
Autherine Lucy became the first black student admitted to the University of Alabama in February 1956, and she was suspended after white students rioted, and was later expelled.
The arrests of King and dozens of other boycott leaders in February 1956 included an indictment of about eighty-nine people under a state anti-boycott law.
The Montgomery victory was achieved despite the violence, and the bombings and arrests helped to bring the case to national attention and to the federal courts.

notes.h: Assessment: how far did Montgomery bring change?
notes.b: Examiners reward evaluation that weighs the boycott's achievement against its limits and against the views of contemporaries and later historians.
points: Achievement: the bus desegregation ruling and the success of the boycott showed that sustained, organised protest could defeat legal segregation.
Limit: the victory applied only to buses in one city, and it did not change the wider system of segregation or the voting restrictions across Alabama.
Contemporary white opinion in Montgomery condemned the boycott and used intimidation, while many black residents who had suffered segregation for decades saw the victory as long overdue.
Later historians have stressed that the boycott's importance lay in the organisation it created, the leaders it produced and the example it set for other protests.

keyTerms.definition: The organisation formed on 5 December 1955 to co-ordinate the Montgomery bus boycott, with King as its president.
The unequal treatment of black Americans on Montgomery's buses, where segregation rules required them to give up seats to white passengers.
The federal case brought in 1956 challenging Montgomery's bus segregation, which the Supreme Court upheld on 13 November 1956.
The volunteer transport system that carried boycotting passengers to work and school in Montgomery during the boycott.
The Montgomery women's organisation led by Jo Ann Robinson, which called for the boycott and distributed its leaflets.
The strategy used in the Montgomery boycott of peaceful protest and refusal to comply with segregation, without retaliation against violence.
